title: Rumi's world, again
hookLine: a Muslim, a scholar, a lover of God, in his own tradition
tomorrow: a poet named for what he carried by heart. who?

lines: A MUSLIM POET, A CATHOLIC MEMORIAL?
A SCHOLAR AND PREACHER IN KONYA.
cards: Inés's aunt asked it straight out: a Muslim poet, at a Catholic memorial? It's a fair question, and it deserves a real answer. That answer starts by not shrinking Rumi into a greeting card.
Before he was a well-known poet, he was a Muslim scholar and preacher in Konya, teaching the Quran and Islamic law.

teach.b: His followers tell how the Masnavi began. His companion Husam al-Din asked him for a long teaching poem the circle could study.

Rumi reached into his turban and drew out a paper with the opening already written: the song of the reed flute, cut from its reed bed, crying with longing to go home. Here's the teaching under it, from Rumi's own world.
The Quran gives words for when loss strikes, the same line Rumi's ladder closed on a few days ago.
In Pickthall's English: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Sufis hear the reed's cry as the soul's longing for God, the home it came from. Now the neighbor.
Inés's family is Catholic, and Augustine says something close in his Confessions, in Pusey's words: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee."

Shared: a heart made for God, not at rest until it returns. Honestly different: for Augustine the way home runs through Christ; for Rumi, through the Quran, the Prophet and the Sufi path of remembrance.
Two houses, each with its own door.
So the answer for the aunt: Rumi belongs at the memorial as himself, a Muslim speaking from his own world. Not a poet with his faith filed off.

how: Rumi taught as a Muslim scholar in Konya, and the Masnavi is full of the Quran and hadith. Mevlevis today read and sing his poems within Islamic practice, and readers of other faiths read him too.

s: Rumi was a poet first and only later turned religious
he was a Muslim scholar and preacher in Konya before he was a well-known poet.
the Masnavi opens with a reed flute longing for home
his followers say he drew those opening lines from his turban.
Rumi and Augustine say the same thing in the same way
both speak of a heart longing for God, but the way home differs: Christ for Augustine, the Quran and the Sufi path for Rumi.

games.q: a classmate says Rumi was 'spiritual, not religious,' so his faith doesn't matter to the poems. what fits what you heard today?
o: his longing is Islamic: the Quran's 'unto Him we are returning.'
she's right; he left religion behind for love.
his faith matters to Muslims, but not to his poems.
games.why: Rumi was a Muslim scholar; Sufis hear the reed's cry as the soul's return to God, the Quran's own words for loss.

practice: Close your eyes and follow your breath out and back, like a note on a reed. If you pray, you can rest in the words of your own tradition; if not, just notice what your heart is restless for, and leave it unanswered.

wordCard.voice: Rumi's world: Islam, the Quran, the Sufi path of remembrance. The reed's longing comes from there.

orig.note: Persian: the reed flute. The Masnavi opens with its song of longing to go home.

carryVoice: For the road: his own world, read as the Muslim he was. Rumi again, all eight days, done.
